findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Base the derivation comment's 'normal loaded run' on the measured idle WALL range (3-8 s) times 7-8x, not 3.5-4 s, and restate the real headroom factor of 135 s over that figure.
evidence: "Idle cost: one run takes 3-8 s wall and 3-3.5 s CPU at load 30."
"Normal loaded run: idle 3.5-4 s times the measured 7-8x full-suite slowdown, about 27 s."
findings.finding: The 'normal loaded run' estimate takes its idle baseline from CPU time rather than wall time. The plan measures idle at '3-8 s wall and 3-3.5 s CPU', but the derivation uses 'idle 3.5-4 s times the measured 7-8x full-suite slowdown, about 27 s'. Using the measured idle wall upper bound of 8 s, 7-8x gives about 56-64 s. That is what the old 60 s bound produced, and it is only about 2x below 135 s, not the 5x the comment claims.
findings.location: Approach — derivation comment bullet 1; Root cause — Idle cost
scenarios: A run at the slow end of idle wall time (8 s) under a 7-8x full-suite slowdown reaches about 64 s, which matches the observed failures and leaves much less margin than the comment says.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In the Approach section, say why SCRIPT_RUN_TIMEOUT has no runtime override, unlike the CPython/Bazel/Go/lit timeouts it cites (e.g. the repo's config-ownership policy against env settings), so the deviation is a recorded, justified choice.
evidence: Plan: "after comparing CPython (test.support LOOPBACK/SHORT/LONG_TIMEOUT), Bazel (test size timeouts), Go (-timeout), LLVM lit and pytest-timeout practice"

Retrieved docs.python.org/3/library/test.html: "SHORT_TIMEOUT ... The timeout value depends on the regrtest --timeout command line option. If a test using SHORT_TIMEOUT starts to fail randomly on slow buildbots, use LONG_TIMEOUT instead."
The repo has tests/scripts/test_check_config_ownership.py (fixture `TIMEOUT = os.getenv('SOME_KNOB')`), which hints at a local policy against env settings, but the plan doesn't cite it as the reason.
findings.finding: The plan cites CPython, Bazel, Go and lit as prior art. All of them let you scale or override the timeout when tests run (CPython's tiers come from `regrtest --timeout`). The plan instead fixes the tier in code and forbids any override, and it gives no reason for departing from the systems it cites.
findings.location: Approach (operator decision, 2026-11-17): "The scale lives in code. There is no environment variable, config key or CLI flag."
scenarios: A future host is even more loaded than the measured 40-70 load average, so runs go past 135 s. With no rationale recorded, a maintainer may add an env override that undoes the operator decision or breaks the config-ownership check.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence after "The scale lives in code": "Unlike CPython's regrtest --timeout or Bazel's --test_timeout, no override is offered because <repo policy / config-ownership check reason>. A future change in load is handled by re-measuring and editing the derivation comment."
